extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, comparative politics, and federalism
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the factors that help sustain or threaten the longevity of a federal union (political, social, economic, geographic, and institutional). Applicable to comparative analysis of federations and the American Union in particular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unequal distribution of benefits among states
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal government would derive its power from the unequal distribution of those benefits among the states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advantages produced by union are distributed very unequally, the central authority gains power because some states become more dependent on it or it can legitimize actions as serving the whole while really serving dominant interests. Example/anti-pattern: a confederation where benefits concentrate in some states risks centralization under the pretext of union sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preponderance of a single state leading to dominance
rubrics_metrics.description: If one of the confederated states have acquired a preponderance sufficiently great to enable it to take exclusive possession of the central authority, it will consider the other states as subject provinces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large or powerful member states that outgrow others can seize control of federal institutions and use federal authority to secure their supremacy. This undermines the confederation's equality and effectively ends genuine union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency toward centralization when confederation principles are abandoned
rubrics_metrics.description: The power which acts in the name of the confederation becomes stronger the more it abandons the natural state and the acknowledged principles of confederations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As the central government departs from decentralized/confederal norms, it consolidates authority; this may produce activity done in the name of the Union though the federal government 'will have ceased to exist' in spirit. Monitor degree of centralization as an indicator of constitutional change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary continued membership of states
rubrics_metrics.description: The present Union will only last as long as the states which compose it choose to continue members of the confederation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Durability depends on ongoing consent; if a portion seriously desires separation, the Union cannot indefinitely prevent it. Political cohesion thus relies on states' perception that union remains in their interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal enforcement through judiciary and executive (laws operate on individuals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The acts of the general government operate through the judiciary, upon individual citizens, and not upon the states; courts act upon individuals and the executive/military must intervene if their judgments are resisted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective legal and executive mechanisms that can enforce federal laws against individuals (and, if necessary, against resisting state authorities) strengthen the Union by ensuring federal acts have practical effect. The editor notes this was demonstrated during the tariff controversy with South Carolina.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial interdependence and external strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans, although isolated on their continent, require strength for commerce; remaining united preserves strength toward foreign nations and prevents foreign powers from establishing footholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shared commercial interests and the need for international security (e.g., a powerful navy) bind regions together. Dissolution would create inland custom-houses, trade barriers, and burdens like standing armies and new taxes; thus common external economic interests favor union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of natural geographic barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: No natural barrier exists in the regions inhabited by the Anglo-Americans; features like the Alleganies do not form necessary limits of different states and open easy passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geographic continuity and easy internal communication reduce separateness of regions and favor political unity. Conversely, strong natural barriers can promote separate national development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic complementarity across regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Union is the means by which different sources of wealth (agricultural south, commercial/manufacturing north, mixed west) are opened to all and rendered equally advantageous to the several districts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When regions' economic outputs complement each other and rely on shared markets (raw materials, manufacturing, shipping), material interests align in favor of maintaining the union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared political and civic principles
rubrics_metrics.description: From Maine to the Floridas... the people is held to be the legitimate source of all power. The same notions are entertained respecting liberty and equality, the liberty of the press, the right of association, the jury, and the responsibility of the agents of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform acceptance of basic constitutional and civic principles across member states creates a powerful cohesive force. Assess commonality of such principles when judging union durability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared moral/philosophical attitudes and public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Anglo-Americans acknowledge the absolute moral authority of the reason of the community... they hold that public opinion is the surest arbiter of what is lawful or forbidden, true or false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convergence in moral outlook, belief in progress and public opinion's authority, and shared views on self-government support social cohesion beyond mere material interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: National pride and sense of distinct identity
rubrics_metrics.description: They are separated from all other nations by a common feeling of pride... they conceive an overweening opinion of their superiority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A common national self-regard can both unite internally (shared pride) and separate the population from outside influences; this identity reinforces cohesion but may also breed complacency or exceptionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural and character differences (especially due to slavery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Slavery has not created interests in the south contrary to those of the north, but it has modified the character and changed the habits of the natives of the south... the citizen of the southern states is invested with a sort of domestic dictatorship; the northern citizen becomes patient, reflecting, tolerant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences in manners, habits, and civic character arising from institutions (e.g., slavery) produce social divergence that can lead to misunderstanding, friction, and eventual political conflict even when economic interests align. Monitor cultural divergence as an indirect threat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population growth and increase in number/size of states
rubrics_metrics.description: The Union grew from thirteen to twenty-four members; population tripled in forty years. When states grow large or the number of states multiplies, unanimity is diminished and states feel less existential dependence on the union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid demographic expansion and the creation of many or very large member states reduce the perceived necessity of union and increase the chance of rivalry and ambition; size and number are risk factors for cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of frontier settlers and western representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Settlers who are constantly peopling the valley of the Mississippi are adventurers impatient of restraint... they are unknown to each other and have neither traditions nor family feeling... nevertheless they exercise a great influence in its councils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newly settled frontier populations often have weaker institutional habits and different characters, yet gain political influence before social stabilization; their representation can destabilize established political cultures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shifting internal balance of power due to territorial expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: The relative position of the central federal power is continually displaced... the great body of the people is advancing inland... the basin of the Mississippi is marked out as the future centre of the federal government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Westward expansion and differential population growth shift political majorities and centers of influence, altering policy directions and interregional balances; these shifts can create tensions between founding regions and new majorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional disparities in natural advantages and economic opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: The north is superior to the south both in commerce and manufacture... shores of the Atlantic are half-peopled with land held by owners, while western states offer boundless fields; the Mississippi valley is more fertile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uneven geographic endowments and settlement opportunities produce divergent growth rates. Rapidly developing regions gain relative power and may pursue different interests, threatening unanimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human passions: rivalry, ambition, and pursuit of independent designs
rubrics_metrics.description: A government is called upon to hold together forty different peoples... to avoid all rivalry, ambition, and struggles, between them, and to direct their independent activity to the accomplishment of the same designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The perennial forces of ambition and rivalry among peoples/states make perfect, long-term cohesion unlikely; institutional checks and shared incentives are needed to mitigate these human tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynamic and continual territorial changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Continual changes which take place in the position of its internal strength... towns are founded from day to day, and states almost from year to year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ongoing territorial growth and administrative reconfiguration create moving political dynamics that complicate stable governance; anticipate and plan for new states, shifting populations, and evolving interests.
